sections.h2: What is an immersive meditation?
p: An immersive meditation is a complete guided visualization set in one imaginary place. Instead of watching your breath alone, you walk through a scene with all your senses. You hear rain on old stone, feel warm sand under your feet and see candlelight on ancient walls.

Each of the 17 worlds in MeditaDream follows the same gentle shape. You arrive in an opening scene, explore it, live one meaningful moment, then come back. Along the way, you do a few small things: rest a hand on a door, follow an animal, receive an object to keep.

sections.h2: Why a guided meditation journey calms the mind
p: A busy mind rarely goes quiet on command. Telling yourself to stop thinking usually brings more thoughts. A guided meditation journey works differently: it gives your attention something rich and gentle to hold.

Psychologists call this capacity absorption: being so taken by an experience that everything else fades into the background. You know it from a good novel or a favorite piece of music. In a meditation journey, the scene does the holding, and you simply follow.
This is why an inner journey can feel restful even when a lot happens in it. You are not trying to empty your mind. You are giving it a calm, beautiful place to be, for about a quarter of an hour.
sections.tip: If your mind wanders, that is normal. Come back to one detail of the scene, a sound or a color, and keep going.

astral.lead: Floating above your own body and looking down at the room: for many people, it is a lifelong curiosity. Here is what astral projection means, where the idea comes from, what science has observed and how people practice it.
astral.def: **Astral projection** is the experience of feeling your awareness leave your physical body and perceive from outside it. sections.h2: Astral projection meaning: the key words
p: The astral projection definition is simple: you feel that your awareness has left your body, and you perceive from somewhere outside it. People often describe seeing their body from above, or floating near the ceiling.

The word astral comes from the Latin for “of the stars.” It reflects an old idea: a subtle body made of finer, luminous matter. Around it, a whole vocabulary has grown. The meaning of an out-of-body experience is purely descriptive, while astral projection carries a spiritual view of the world.
cards: Astral projection
The deliberate attempt to leave the body in awareness, usually from deep relaxation, at the edge of sleep.
Astral travel
Often used as a synonym. It stresses the journey itself: moving through rooms, landscapes or other realms once you feel separated.
Out-of-body experience
The neutral, scientific term, often shortened to OBE. It describes perceiving from outside your body, whatever the cause.
Astral body
In esoteric traditions, the subtle double said to carry your awareness. Many authors describe a silver cord linking it to the physical body.
Astral plane
Also called the astral realm: the dimension this double is said to travel through, often described as fluid and shaped by thought.

sections.h2: Where the idea of astral travel comes from
p: The idea that part of us can travel without the body is very old. Many cultures tell of a soul or a double that wanders during sleep or trance. Ancient Egypt, for example, described the ba, a part of the person able to leave the tomb and move about.

The modern vocabulary comes from Theosophy. The Theosophical Society, founded in New York in 1875 by Helena Blavatsky and Henry Steel Olcott, spread the terms astral body and astral plane. In its model, a person has several subtle bodies, and the astral one carries feelings and desires.

In the twentieth century, the American Robert Monroe brought the subject to a wide audience. His 1971 book, Journeys Out of the Body, describes his own experiences in plain language. It helped popularize the phrase out-of-body experience, and Monroe later founded the Monroe Institute in Virginia.

sections.h2: Is astral projection real? What science has observed
p: Out-of-body experiences are real experiences, whatever their cause. Many people report at least one in their lifetime, often by surprise, at the edge of sleep or in deep relaxation.

In 2002, Olaf Blanke and his colleagues described a striking case in the journal Nature. Stimulating the right angular gyrus, a region of the brain, made one woman feel she was floating above her body. Later work linked OBEs to the way the brain combines vision, balance and body sensations.

Some researchers have also hidden targets in rooms to test what people perceive during an OBE, and the results remain debated. These findings show that the brain can create the feeling of being outside the body. Whether anything actually leaves is a matter of belief, not measurement.
sections.tip: You can practice either way: as an exploration of consciousness, or as a spiritual path. The exercises are the same.

sections.h2: What does astral projection feel like?
p: Reports vary from person to person, but some sensations come up again and again. Knowing them in advance makes them less surprising, and practitioners say that staying calm helps the experience last.
ul: Vibrations or a buzzing that spreads through the body, sometimes with a rushing sound.
Heaviness, then sudden lightness, as if the body were sinking or floating.
A sense of swaying, rolling or slipping sideways.
Seeing the room with your eyes closed, often a little differently from how it really looks.
The feeling of a double sitting up, rising or hovering near the ceiling.
Waking up unable to move for a few seconds, sometimes with a strong sense of presence.

sections.h2: How to astral project: classic techniques for beginners
p: If you are wondering how to astral project, most methods share the same base: a deeply relaxed body and an awake mind. People usually practice lying down, at the edge of sleep, or after waking early in the morning. Here is the sequence that astral projection for beginners often follows.
steps: Relax deeply
Lie on your back and release your body area by area. Let it grow so still that you almost stop feeling it.
Stay awake inside
Keep a quiet, alert attention, like a light left on in a dark house. Most attempts happen at this edge between sleep and waking.
The rope
Imagine a rope hanging above you. Climb it hand over hand with imaginary arms, without moving your physical ones. Robert Bruce popularized this method in his book Astral Dynamics.
The roll-out
Imagine rolling sideways out of your body, the way you would roll off a mattress, without moving a muscle. Monroe described this approach.
The imaginary fall
Feel yourself sinking or falling gently backward, and let the sensation carry you toward separation.
The target
Before you begin, choose a familiar place or object. Once relaxed, picture yourself there in vivid detail.
sections.warn: Do not force it. Most attempts end in sleep or simply in calm rest, which is fine. Note what you felt, and try again another day.

sections.h2: Astral projection vs lucid dreaming
p: The two experiences are close cousins, and some people move from one to the other in the same night. The difference lies mostly in how they begin and how they are explained. Astral dreaming is a name some people use for experiences that fall in between.
If dreams are your natural doorway, our guide to [lucid dreaming](/en/lucid-dreaming-meditation.html) explains the main techniques, from the dream journal to WBTB.

sections.h2: Is astral projection dangerous?
p: Practiced as meditation, astral projection is deep relaxation combined with imagination. There is no evidence that anyone can get stuck outside the body, and you can always open your eyes. The real challenges are fear, frustration and lost sleep.

Astral projection and sleep paralysis often go together. During REM sleep, your muscles stay relaxed so that you do not act out your dreams. If you wake before this ends, you may be unable to move for a few seconds and sense a presence. It is frightening, but it passes.
ul: If you wake up unable to move, breathe slowly and wiggle a finger or a toe.
Ground yourself afterward: feel your weight, touch the floor, drink a glass of water.
Practice when you are well rested, not on nights when sleep is precious.
On days when you feel fragile, choose a calming session from [Body, Calm & Sleep](/en/meditations/guided-sleep-meditation.html) instead.
sections.warn: If these experiences frighten you, disturb your nights or keep coming back, ask a professional for advice.

faq: What is astral projection?

Astral projection is the experience of feeling your awareness leave your body and perceive from outside it. Esoteric traditions say a subtle astral body travels through an astral plane. Science studies the same experience under the name out-of-body experience, without ruling on whether anything leaves. People usually practice it lying down, in deep relaxation, at the edge of sleep.
How do I astral project for the first time?

Choose a time when you are well rested, such as early morning or a quiet afternoon. Lie on your back, relax your body completely and keep your mind gently alert. Then try one technique, such as the rope or the roll-out, for a few minutes, without forcing. Most first attempts end in calm rest or sleep. Note what you felt and try again another day.
Is astral projection dangerous?

Practiced as guided meditation, astral projection is deep relaxation combined with imagination. There is no evidence that anyone gets stuck outside the body. The main difficulties are fear, especially during sleep paralysis, and losing sleep through too many night attempts. Ground yourself after each session. If it weighs on you or keeps happening, ask a professional for advice.
What does astral projection feel like?

People often describe vibrations or buzzing, a sudden lightness, a sense of rolling or floating, and the feeling of looking at the room from above. Some see their own body. Others feel a double rising without seeing anything. The experience can be brief and dreamlike. Many practitioners say that staying calm is what lets it last a little longer.
What is the astral plane?

In Theosophy and later esoteric teachings, the astral plane, or astral realm, is a dimension of finer matter where the astral body is said to travel. It is often described as fluid, luminous and shaped by thought and feeling. This is a spiritual model, not a scientific finding. In meditation, you can explore it as an inner landscape.
What is the difference between astral projection and lucid dreaming?

Astral projection usually starts from waking: you relax deeply and feel yourself leave the body, often in your own room. A lucid dream starts inside a dream, when you realize you are dreaming. Sleep research has confirmed lucid dreaming. Astral projection is studied as an out-of-body experience, and its interpretation remains a matter of belief.
What did the CIA say about astral projection?

In 1983, a US Army report analyzed the Gateway Process, a set of techniques from the Monroe Institute. The CIA declassified the document in 2003, and it later became popular online. It offers a speculative theory of how the techniques might work. It is an analysis of a method, not proof that astral projection is real.
How long does it take to learn how to astral travel?

There is no fixed timeline. Some people have a spontaneous experience early, while others practice for months and mostly find deep relaxation. Short, regular sessions tend to work better than long, tense attempts. See the relaxation itself as the practice, and any feeling of separation as a bonus.

sections.h2: What are chakras? Chakra meaning and origins
p: In Sanskrit, cakra means “wheel” or “circle.” The word describes centers where, according to tradition, channels of subtle energy meet and turn. These channels are called nadis, and the life energy that flows through them is called prana.
Chakras come from the tantric traditions of India, both Hindu and Buddhist. The texts do not agree on their number: some systems describe four centers, others six, seven or more.

The seven-chakra map most people know today rests largely on one text, the Ṣaṭ-cakra-nirūpaṇa, written by Pūrṇānanda in 1577. It describes six centers, plus a thousand-petaled lotus at the crown. In 1919, the British scholar John Woodroffe, writing as Arthur Avalon, translated it in The Serpent Power. That book shaped how Western readers came to know the chakras.

sections.h2: The 7 chakras and their meanings, from root to crown
p: Here is each chakra with its Sanskrit name, its place in the body and the themes modern teachers associate with it. The petals, seed sounds and elements come from the traditional texts. The colors are a modern addition.
cards: Root chakra, Muladhara
Its name means “root support.” At the base of the spine, it stands for grounding and safety. Four petals, seed sound lam, element earth. Modern color: red.
Sacral chakra, Svadhisthana
“One's own place,” in the lower belly. It is linked to pleasure, creativity and the flow of emotions. Six petals, seed sound vam, element water. Modern color: orange.
Solar plexus chakra, Manipura
The “city of jewels,” above the navel. It carries will, confidence and inner fire. Ten petals, seed sound ram, element fire. Modern color: yellow.
Heart chakra, Anahata
“Unstruck,” like a sound that needs no blow. In the center of the chest, it is linked to love and compassion. Twelve petals, seed sound yam, element air. Modern color: green.
Throat chakra, Vishuddha
“Especially pure,” at the throat. It stands for expression, listening and truthfulness. Sixteen petals, seed sound ham, element space. Modern color: blue.
Third eye chakra, Ajna
“Command” or “perception,” between the eyebrows. It is the seat of intuition and inner vision. Two petals, seed sound om. Modern color: indigo.
Crown chakra, Sahasrara
The “thousand-petaled” lotus, at the top of the head. It points to awareness and unity beyond the self. Modern color: violet or white.

sections.h2: Chakra colors: where the rainbow comes from
p: If you have seen a chakra chart, you know the seven colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. They are easy to remember, and they make a beautiful image. But you will not find them in the old texts.
The traditional sources give each lotus its own colors, and they do not follow the order of the rainbow. The rainbow sequence is a Western association of the twentieth century.

Today, it is part of how most people learn the chakras. You can use the colors as a simple support for imagery, while knowing they are a modern addition. If a different color comes to you in meditation, there is nothing wrong with it.

sections.h2: Blocked, open, balanced: what chakra balancing means
p: Many books describe a blocked chakra as a center where energy no longer flows well, and an open chakra as one where it flows freely. Chakra balancing means bringing all seven back into harmony. These are images from a spiritual tradition, not measurements.

In meditation, these images become something practical. You rest your attention on one area of the body, breathe there and notice what you feel. You may picture a color, a turning wheel or a soft light. A tight throat or a warm chest simply becomes something to observe.

What people mean by chakra healing usually lies here: a calm, attentive time spent with each center, often with breath and imagery. It is a practice of well-being and attention. It is not a way to repair the body, and the sessions in the app make no such promise.
sections.tip: Do not try to work out which chakra is blocked. Simply notice which areas feel easy to sense and which feel vague, and give the vague ones a little more time.

sections.h2: Kundalini: the energy coiled at the base of the spine
p: In tantric yoga, kundalini is a dormant energy coiled at the base of the spine, often pictured as a sleeping serpent. Practices aim to awaken it so that it rises through the central channel, the sushumna, to the crown. This is the journey The Serpent Power describes.

Kundalini practice traditionally involves intense breathing, postures and long training with a teacher. The chakra meditations in the app are much gentler. They work with attention and imagery, not with forceful techniques. For a calm way to sense the body as light, Light Body Expansion, in [Cosmic & Void](/en/meditations/non-dual-awareness-meditation.html), lasts 31 minutes.
sections.warn: Strong breathing practices can bring up intense sensations or emotions. Go slowly, and if anything weighs on you or keeps returning, ask a professional for advice.

sections.h2: Are chakras real? What science says
p: Chakras are not anatomical structures. Dissection and imaging have never found them, and they do not match any specific organ. Some authors compare their positions to major nerve clusters along the spine, but that is a modern interpretation.

Researchers do study interoception, the sense of the body's inner state: heartbeat, breath, warmth, tension. Meditation trains exactly this kind of attention. The chakras offer it a clear path to follow, one point at a time.

So you can approach the chakras in two ways: as a spiritual map with deep roots, or simply as seven points of attention along the body. Both work for meditation, and you do not need to believe anything to begin.

sections.h2: How to do a chakra meditation
p: This simple chakra meditation takes about fifteen minutes, seated or lying down. For a fully guided version, the [Body, Calm & Sleep](/en/meditations/guided-sleep-meditation.html) category includes the app's chakra sessions.
steps: Settle
Sit with a long spine, or lie on your back. Take a few slow breaths and feel your weight.
Begin at the root
Rest your attention at the base of the spine. Breathe there for a minute. If it helps, picture a warm red glow.
Climb center by center
Move to the lower belly, the navel, the chest, the throat, the point between the eyebrows and the top of the head. Give each one a few breaths.
Notice without fixing
Some areas feel clear, others vague. Let them be as they are. The noticing is the practice.
See the whole line
Feel the seven points together, like beads on a thread from base to crown.
Come back down
Bring your attention back to your feet and the ground before you open your eyes.

sections.h2: How to open your third eye in meditation
p: How to open your third eye is one of the most searched questions about chakras. In tradition, Ajna is the seat of inner vision, and opening it means seeing more clearly within. Some modern authors link it to the pineal gland, which Descartes called the principal seat of the soul.

In practice, third eye meditation is gentle. Rest your attention between the eyebrows, without squinting, and watch the dark space behind your closed eyes. Images may appear, or not. Stay curious rather than eager.

They range from The Third Eye and the Two Physical Eyes to The Mandala that Builds Itself. To strengthen your inner images first, see our guide to [guided imagery](/en/guided-imagery-visualization.html). And if you enjoy subtle sensations in motion, [qigong](/en/qigong.html) works with energy centers of its own.

faq: What are the 7 chakras?

The 7 chakras are centers of subtle energy described by the yogic and tantric traditions of India. From the base of the spine upward, they are Muladhara (root), Svadhisthana (sacral), Manipura (solar plexus) and Anahata (heart). Then come Vishuddha (throat), Ajna (third eye) and Sahasrara (crown). Each one is linked to a theme, from grounding to spiritual connection.
What color is each chakra?

In the modern system, the root chakra is red, the sacral chakra orange and the solar plexus chakra yellow. The heart chakra is green, the throat chakra blue, the third eye indigo and the crown violet or white. These rainbow colors are a Western association of the twentieth century. The old tantric texts describe the lotuses with other colors.
How do you balance your chakras?

In meditation, chakra balancing usually means visiting each center with calm attention. You breathe into each area, from the root to the crown, and notice what you feel without trying to fix it. Many people add a color or a turning wheel as imagery. See it as a practice of attention and well-being, with no promise about the body.
What is a blocked chakra?

In spiritual teaching, a blocked chakra is a center where energy is said to flow poorly. People often link it to the chakra's theme, such as a blocked throat chakra and difficulty speaking up. This is a symbolic language, not a measurable state. In meditation, you can simply notice which areas feel vague and give them gentle attention.
How do I open my third eye?

Sit comfortably, close your eyes and rest your attention between your eyebrows, without straining. Breathe slowly and watch the dark space in front of you. Images, colors or nothing at all may appear, and all of that is fine. Short, regular sessions work better than long, forced ones. The Third Eye category in the app guides you through five sessions.
Are chakras real?

Chakras are not physical organs, and science has not found them in the body. They belong to the spiritual traditions of India, where they describe the subtle body. Many people still find them useful as a map for attention: seven points along the spine to explore, one after another. You do not need to believe in them to meditate with them.
What is kundalini?

In tantric yoga, kundalini is an energy said to lie coiled at the base of the spine, like a sleeping serpent. Traditional practices aim to awaken it so that it rises through each chakra to the crown. These practices can be intense and are usually learned with an experienced teacher. Gentle chakra meditation is a calmer place to start.

qigong.h1: What is qigong? Benefits, exercises and how to start
qigong.lead: Slow movements, deep breathing, a quiet mind: qigong has been practiced in China for centuries, in parks at dawn and in quiet rooms. Here is what it is, how it differs from tai chi and how to begin at home.
qigong.def: **Qigong** is a Chinese practice that combines slow movement or still postures, regulated breathing and focused attention. The name joins qi, meaning breath or vital energy, and gong, meaning work or skill. It is often translated as “energy work.” Also spelled qi gong, chi gong or chi kung, it is practiced for calm, balance and self-cultivation.

sections.h2: What is qigong? The meaning of qi and gong
p: Qi (气) is one of the central ideas of Chinese thought. The character first evoked vapor or breath. Over time, it came to mean the vital energy that animates all living things. Many English speakers write it chi, which is why you will see “chi energy” and “chi gong.”

Gong (功) means work, skill or achievement: something gained through steady effort. The same word appears in kung fu, gongfu in Chinese. Qigong is therefore the steady cultivation of breath and energy, practiced day after day.

The spellings vary with the system used to write Chinese in Latin letters. Qigong and qi gong follow pinyin, the system used in China today. Chi kung comes from the older Wade-Giles system, and chi gong mixes the two.

sections.h2: A short history of qigong
p: The practice is far older than its name. Ancient Chinese texts describe daoyin, “guiding and pulling,” exercises that combine movement and breath. A painting on silk found in a Han dynasty tomb at Mawangdui, sealed in 168 BCE, shows dozens of figures performing them.

Over the centuries, Daoist, Buddhist and martial traditions each developed their own methods. Famous sets emerged along the way. The Five Animals Frolics is attributed to Hua Tuo, a celebrated figure of the late Han dynasty. The Ba Duan Jin, or Eight Brocades, is attested since the Song dynasty.

The word qigong itself was popularized in China in the 1950s, as a common name for these many practices. It later spread around the world. In the app, The Taoist Sanctuary in the Mountains, in [Sacred Places](/en/meditations/sacred-places-guided-meditation.html), takes you to such a retreat at dawn, above a sea of clouds.

sections.h2: The three regulations: body, breath and mind
p: Chinese teachers often sum up qigong in three regulations, or tiáo. You regulate the body, the breath and the mind, and the practice happens when all three come together.
No single one is enough on its own. A perfect posture with a restless mind is just exercise. A calm mind in a slumped body is just rest. Qigong lives where the three meet.

Chinese tradition also has energy centers of its own, the dantian. The lower dantian, below the navel, is where many exercises gather attention, much as Indian traditions work with the [7 chakras](/en/chakra-meditation.html).

sections.h2: Main types of qigong
p: There are many qigong styles, but they fall into a few broad families. Most of them mix several of these aspects.
cards: Moving qigong
Slow, flowing sequences coordinated with the breath, like the Eight Brocades or the Five Animals.
Still qigong
Postures held without moving, seated, lying or standing, where the work is entirely inward.
Qigong for well-being
Gentle daily sets aimed at suppleness, balance and calm. This is the form most people practice.
Martial qigong
Practices that support the martial arts by building rootedness, power and resilience.
Meditative qigong
Daoist and Buddhist methods centered on stillness, inner circulation and self-cultivation.
sections.tip: Standing qigong deserves a special mention. In zhan zhuang, “standing like a post,” often called standing like a tree, you hold one simple posture for several minutes, and it goes surprisingly deep.

sections.h2: Ba Duan Jin: the Eight Brocades and other classic sets
p: The Ba Duan Jin is one of the most widely practiced qigong sets in the world. Its name means “eight pieces of brocade,” as if each movement were a precious silk. It is short, gentle and easy to fit into a morning. Names vary from one translation to another, but the eight movements are usually these:
ul: Two Hands Hold Up the Heavens
Drawing the Bow to Shoot the Hawk
Separating Heaven and Earth
The Wise Owl Gazes Backward
Swaying the Head and Shaking the Tail
Two Hands Reach Down to the Feet
Clenching the Fists with an Angry Gaze
Rising and Falling on the Toes
sections.tip: Other classic sets include the Five Animals Frolics, which imitates the tiger, deer, bear, monkey and crane. The Yi Jin Jing, another classic, is traditionally linked to the Shaolin temple.

sections.h2: Tai chi vs qigong: what is the difference?
p: Tai chi and qigong look alike: both are slow, flowing and centered on the breath. Many teachers even see tai chi as a form of qigong. The main differences lie in their purpose and their complexity.
If you are starting from scratch, qigong is usually the easier door. You can learn a single movement today and practice it tomorrow morning.

sections.h2: Qigong benefits: what research describes
p: Qigong is popular for how it makes people feel: calmer, more supple, more at home in their body. Research has started to look at these effects, often together with tai chi.

Studies have mostly looked at balance, flexibility, relaxation and attention. Results are often encouraging, but many studies are small and their methods vary. No study can promise anything to a given person.

What you can count on is simpler. A slow, regular practice offers a daily moment of calm, a closer sense of your body and a breath that has time to slow down. If the breath is your way in, Breathing with the Whole Body, in [Body, Calm & Sleep](/en/meditations/guided-sleep-meditation.html), lasts 13 minutes.

sections.h2: Qigong for beginners: three simple exercises
p: Practicing qigong at home is easy: a quiet corner is all you need. These qigong exercises take five to ten minutes, with no equipment. Morning qigong is a long tradition, so try them after waking, near an open window. Wear loose clothes and stand with your feet hip-width apart, knees soft.

For guided practice, the [Sensations & Qigong](/en/meditations/qigong-meditation.html) category offers four sessions built on the same ideas. Afterward, [Monastery at Sunrise](/en/worlds/himalayan-monastery-sunrise-meditation.html), a world made for the morning, can carry the calm into your day.
steps: Warming the hands
Rub your palms together for a few seconds, then hold them slightly apart. Feel the warmth, the tingling or the gentle pull between them, as if you were holding a ball of air.
Holding up the heavens
Interlace your fingers in front of your belly. Inhale as you raise your hands above your head, palms up. Exhale as you lower your arms out to the sides. Repeat six to eight times.
Standing like a tree
Raise your arms in front of your chest, rounded as if hugging a tree. Let your weight sink into your feet. Breathe slowly and stay for one to three minutes.
Closing
Rest both hands on your lower belly, below the navel, and take three slow breaths before you move on with your day.

faq: What is qigong?

Qigong is a Chinese practice that combines slow movement or still postures, regulated breathing and focused attention. Its name joins qi, breath or vital energy, and gong, work or skill. It grew out of ancient exercises called daoyin and took its modern name in 1950s China. Today it is practiced around the world for calm, balance and self-cultivation.
What is the difference between tai chi and qigong?

Tai chi is a martial art built on a long, choreographed sequence called a form, which takes months to learn. Qigong is broader and simpler: often a few movements repeated, or a posture held in stillness, with a strong focus on the breath. Many teachers consider tai chi a form of qigong. Beginners usually find qigong easier to start.
Is qigong good for beginners?

Yes. Qigong for beginners can be as simple as one movement repeated slowly with the breath. There is no complex choreography to memorize, and most exercises can be adapted to your range of motion, standing or seated. Start with a few minutes a day, move gently and stay within what feels comfortable.
How long should you practice qigong?

Ten to twenty minutes a day is a good rhythm for most people. Regularity matters more than length: a short daily practice usually feels richer than one long session a week. Many people like morning qigong, right after waking. The guided sessions in the app last 20 to 25 minutes, and the Timer suits shorter practice.
What is chi energy?

Chi, or qi, is the vital energy that Chinese tradition sees flowing through all living things. In the body, it is said to move along channels called meridians and to gather in centers called dantian. Science has not measured qi as a physical energy. In practice, many people experience it as warmth, tingling or a feeling of fullness during qigong.
What are the Eight Brocades?

The Eight Brocades, or Ba Duan Jin, is a classic qigong set of eight movements, attested since the Song dynasty. Its name compares each movement to a piece of fine silk brocade. It includes Two Hands Hold Up the Heavens and Drawing the Bow to Shoot the Hawk. It is short, gentle and one of the most practiced qigong sets in the world.
What is qigong meditation?

Qigong meditation is the still side of qigong. You sit or stand without moving, regulate your breath and guide your attention through the body, often to the lower belly or along an inner circuit. The Small Circulation, a 22-minute session in the app, follows this kind of path. It is calmer than moving qigong, but just as attentive.

reve.lead: You are flying over a city, and suddenly you realize: this is a dream. That moment of clarity is a lucid dream. Here is what science knows about it, the techniques people use most and how to start tonight, calmly.
reve.def: **Lucid dreaming** is being aware that you are dreaming while the dream continues. You stay asleep, usually in REM sleep, yet part of your mind recognizes the dream for what it is. sections.h2: What is lucid dreaming?
p: In an ordinary dream, you accept everything: talking cats, rooms that change shape, your childhood home in another city. In a lucid dream, something clicks. You notice that this cannot be real, and you realize you are dreaming.

The Dutch writer Frederik van Eeden coined the term in 1913. Lucid here means clear: your mind becomes clear inside the dream. Lucidity comes in degrees. It may last a few seconds before you wake up, or long enough to look around calmly, fly or control a dream scene for a while.

Vivid dreaming is something else. A dream can be intense and detailed without you knowing that you are dreaming. And what do lucid dreams mean? People give them very different values: a playground, a source of creative ideas, a spiritual practice. Tibetan Buddhism, for instance, has long practiced dream yoga, which uses lucidity as a path of awareness.

sections.h2: What science knows: from Hearne to LaBerge
p: For a long time, scientists doubted that lucid dreams were real. How could anyone prove they were aware while asleep? The answer came from the eyes. During REM sleep, most muscles are relaxed, but the eyes still move freely.

In 1975, at the University of Hull in England, Keith Hearne recorded the first signals sent from inside a lucid dream. His volunteer, Alan Worsley, moved his eyes left and right in a pattern agreed in advance. At that moment, the sleep recording showed he was in REM sleep.

In the early 1980s, Stephen LaBerge confirmed the method at Stanford University and helped turn lucid dreaming into a field of study. He also developed one of the best-known techniques, MILD. Since then, brain studies have suggested that frontal areas linked to self-reflection become more active during lucidity.

sections.h2: The best time for a lucid dream: your sleep cycles
p: A night of sleep is made of cycles of roughly 90 minutes. Each cycle moves from light sleep into deep sleep, then into REM sleep, when most vivid dreams happen. Early in the night, deep sleep dominates. Toward morning, REM periods grow longer.

This is why the last hours of the night are the best window for lucid dreams. It is also why several techniques ask you to wake up after about five hours of sleep, then go back to bed with a clear intention.

sections.h2: How to lucid dream: the main techniques
p: If you want to know how to have a lucid dream, start with dream recall, then add one technique at a time. These lucid dream techniques are among the most widely used. None of them guarantees a result, but together they invite you to pay closer attention to your nights.
steps: Keep a dream journal
Write down your dreams as soon as you wake up, even a single image. Recall improves with practice, and you begin to notice your dream signs: places, people or situations that come back.
Do reality checks

Several times a day, pause and ask yourself whether you are dreaming. Look at your hands, or read a line of text twice. In dreams, these often change. Done sincerely, the habit can carry into your dreams.
MILD

Mnemonic Induction of Lucid Dreams, developed by LaBerge. When you wake from a dream, replay it and repeat: “Next time I'm dreaming, I will remember that I'm dreaming.” Then picture yourself becoming lucid in that dream.
WBTB
Wake Back to Bed. Set an alarm clock for about five hours after falling asleep. Stay up for a short while, think about lucid dreaming, then go back to bed. It pairs well with MILD.
WILD

Wake-Initiated Lucid Dream. After waking early, you stay aware while your body falls asleep, and enter the dream directly. It is the most demanding technique and can bring sleep paralysis, so try it only once you feel at ease.
sections.tip: Reality checks are a personal habit: the app does not include them. Its role is to help you prepare in the evening and keep your Dream Journal.

sections.h2: Dream journal for lucid dreaming: how to keep one
p: A dream journal is the foundation of every method. A dream you forget leaves no trace, and you cannot recognize patterns you never noticed. In MeditaDream, the Dream Journal has three sections: Dream description, Symbolism & interpretation and Recurring dreams. Everything stays on your phone.
ul: Keep it within reach, and write the moment you wake, before you move or check messages.
Write in the present tense, as if the dream were still happening.
Note feelings and colors, not only events.
Give each dream a short title so you can find it again.
Underline anything strange: these are your dream signs.
Once a week, read back and look for what recurs.

sections.h2: Sleep paralysis: why it scares and how to stay calm
p: During REM sleep, your brain keeps most muscles relaxed so that you do not act out your dreams. Sometimes you wake up before this ends. For a few seconds, or a little longer, you are aware but cannot move.

It can be frightening, because the dreaming brain is still partly active. People often feel a weight on the chest, hear buzzing or sense a presence in the room. These sensations are well known, and they pass. Sleep paralysis is common, especially with WILD or after nights of broken sleep.
ul: Remind yourself what it is: a brief overlap of dreaming and waking.
Breathe slowly. Your breath is still yours to guide.
Focus on moving one small thing, such as a finger or a toe.
Some practitioners use it as a doorway into a lucid dream, by relaxing instead of resisting.

sections.h2: Is lucid dreaming dangerous?
p: For most people, lucid dreaming is a safe and fascinating experience. The main risk is losing sleep, because waking in the night too often can leave you tired. Keep techniques like WBTB for a few nights a week, and never sacrifice your rest for them.

Some people feel briefly confused about what was dreamed and what was real. Others find that intense dreams or sleep paralysis make them uneasy about going to bed. If that happens, take a break. On those evenings, a [sleep sound](/en/sleep-sounds.html) or a session from [Body, Calm & Sleep](/en/meditations/guided-sleep-meditation.html) is a gentler choice.
sections.warn: If your dreams or nights weigh on you, or if sleep paralysis keeps coming back, ask a professional for advice.

sections.h2: Lucid dreaming, guided waking dream and astral projection
p: These three experiences are often confused. They share inner images and a feeling of travel, but they happen in different states.

A guided waking dream trains some skills of lucid dreaming while you are fully awake: staying present inside an inner scene and letting it unfold. Directed Waking Dream, in [Consciousness & Trance](/en/meditations/guided-trance-meditation.html), works this way. faq: What is lucid dreaming?

Lucid dreaming means knowing that you are dreaming while the dream goes on. You remain asleep, usually in REM sleep, but part of your mind is clear and aware. Some lucid dreams last only seconds; others let you explore or steer the dream. Researchers first recorded it in 1975, when a dreamer sent eye signals from inside a dream.
How do you get out of a lucid dream?

Most lucid dreams end on their own, often when excitement wakes you up. To leave on purpose, many people close their dream eyes, blink hard or call out that they want to wake up. Focusing on your physical body, such as your hands resting on the bed, also helps. If you wake into sleep paralysis, breathe slowly and wiggle a finger.
Can I learn how to lucid dream tonight?

Nothing guarantees a lucid dream on a given night, but you can give yourself a real chance. Read your dream journal before bed. Set an alarm for about five hours after falling asleep, stay up briefly, then go back to bed repeating that you will notice you are dreaming. This mix of WBTB and MILD is one of the most popular approaches.
Is lucid dreaming dangerous?

For most people, no. Lucid dreaming happens during normal sleep and is generally considered safe. The main drawbacks are tiredness from waking up too often at night, and fear during episodes of sleep paralysis. Keep night techniques occasional and protect your sleep. If dreams or nights start to weigh on you, take a break and ask a professional for advice.
What causes lucid dreams?

No one knows exactly. Lucid dreams usually arise during REM sleep, when the brain is very active. Brain studies suggest that frontal areas involved in self-reflection become more active during lucidity. Common triggers include noticing something odd in a dream, a strong emotion or an intention set before sleep. Some people have them naturally, while others cultivate them.
How long does it take to have a lucid dream?

It varies widely. Some people have a lucid dream within days of starting a dream journal, while others need weeks or months. A few have had them naturally since childhood. Regular dream recall, reality checks and the MILD technique tend to help most. Stay curious, give it time, and enjoy what you learn about your dreams along the way.
What is the difference between lucid dreaming and astral projection?

A lucid dream begins inside a dream, when you realize you are dreaming, and the scenery can be anything. Astral projection usually begins from waking, with a feeling of leaving your body, often in your own room. Sleep research has confirmed lucid dreaming. Astral projection is studied as an out-of-body experience, and its meaning remains a matter of belief.

sections.h2: What is a shaman? The origin of the word
p: The word shaman comes from Evenki, a Tungusic language of Siberia. Among the Evenki, the šaman is the person who enters trance to communicate with the spirits on behalf of the community. The word reached European languages through Russian.

Anthropologists later used it for similar figures around the world: in Mongolia, among the Sámi of northern Europe, in the Amazon, in North America. Each tradition has its own name, language and rituals. Speaking of shamanism in the singular is a convenience; in reality, there are many shamanisms.

So what does a shaman do? Depending on the culture, a shaman may seek guidance for the group or look for the cause of a misfortune. Some also accompany the souls of the dead or help the hunt. At the heart of it lies the journey: a trance in which the shaman travels in spirit and comes back with something useful.

sections.h2: From Eliade to Harner: shamanism in the West
p: In 1951, the historian of religions Mircea Eliade published the book known in English as Shamanism: Archaic Techniques of Ecstasy. He described the shaman as a specialist of ecstasy, whose soul leaves the body to travel to the sky or the underworld. His work shaped how the West sees shamanism.

In 1980, the American anthropologist Michael Harner published The Way of the Shaman. He drew together elements shared by many cultures: the drum, the journey, the three worlds and the power animal. He called the result core shamanism, a practice without the rituals of any one people.

Core shamanism has made the shamanic path accessible to many, but it also raises questions. Many Indigenous peoples ask that their ceremonies not be copied or sold. The respectful attitude is simple: learn from the source cultures, do not claim their titles and call your practice by its true name.
sections.tip: The sessions in MeditaDream are guided meditations inspired by these traditions. They are not an initiation, and they do not make anyone a shaman.

sections.h2: What is a shamanic trance? Altered states of consciousness
p: A trance is an altered state of consciousness in which attention turns inward and becomes deeply absorbed. The outside world fades, inner images grow vivid and the sense of time shifts. You already know light versions of it, such as being lost in music.

The phrase altered states of consciousness became widely known through a 1969 book of that name, edited by the psychologist Charles Tart. It covers dreaming, hypnosis, meditation and the trance state brought on by rhythm. In the app, the [Consciousness & Trance](/en/meditations/guided-trance-meditation.html) category explores several of these doorways.
In a shamanic trance, the person usually stays aware and remembers the journey. It is less a loss of control than a shift of focus, held by an intention and a rhythm.

sections.h2: Shamanic drumming: the rhythm of the journey
p: In many traditions, the drum carries the journey. In Siberia, it is often called the shaman's horse. Its beat is steady, fast and repetitive, with no melody to follow. Rattles, chanting or dancing can play the same role.

Drumming for a shamanic journey usually follows a simple structure. A steady beat accompanies the traveler for a set time. Then a change in rhythm calls the traveler back, often a few sharp beats followed by a faster roll.

Researchers have studied how repetitive drumming affects attention and brain activity. Small studies suggest that rhythm makes it easier to turn inward and stay absorbed. Science, however, does not describe what the traveler meets.

sections.h2: The three worlds of the shamanic journey
p: Many shamanic traditions describe the universe in three levels, connected by a central axis: a world tree, a mountain or a pillar. The shaman climbs or descends along it. Eliade called it the axis of the world, or axis mundi.

In core shamanism, the lower world is often reached through an opening in the earth, such as a cave, a hollow tree or a spring. The upper world is reached by climbing a tree, a ladder or rising smoke. In the app, Journey to the Lower World and Journey to the Upper World, in [Trances & Techniques](/en/meditations/deep-trance-journey-techniques.html), follow these two paths.

sections.h2: Power animals: finding your power animal
p: A power animal is a protective spirit that appears in animal form and accompanies the shaman. In many cultures, these allies are met during the journey, often in the lower world. Some traditions also link an animal to a person or a clan for life. The word totem, used for these bonds, comes from Ojibwe, a language of North America.

Finding your power animal in a guided meditation is simple. You set the intention, travel inward and notice which animal shows itself, often more than once. It may be humble, like a mouse, or majestic, like a bear. What matters is how it behaves and what it brings you.

The phrase spirit animal comes from Indigenous traditions, and many people now prefer animal guide out of respect. Our page on [spirit guides](/en/spirit-guides.html) explores these figures further. In [The Wolf Spirit Forest](/en/worlds/wolf-spirit-guided-meditation.html), a starry wolf becomes your guide for 15 minutes.

sections.h2: What is a shamanic journey? How a guided journey unfolds
p: A shamanic journey is a trance voyage with a clear intention, made in the imagination and lived with all the senses. Here is how a guided shamanic meditation usually unfolds. For four complete journeys, see the [Shamanic Trance](/en/meditations/shamanic-journey-meditation.html) category.
steps: Prepare the space
Find a quiet, dim room where no one will disturb you. Lie down or sit, and cover your eyes if you like.
State your intention
Choose one simple purpose, such as meeting a protective animal or seeking a symbol for a decision.
Find the entrance
Picture a place you know in nature: a cave, a tree, a pool. It becomes your doorway down or up.
Travel with the drum
Let the rhythm carry you. Follow the path, notice what you see, hear and feel, and let the scene unfold.
Meet and ask
If an animal or a figure appears, greet it, ask your question and accept whatever comes, even silence.
Return by the same path
When the rhythm changes, thank those you met and come back the way you came, to your body and the room.
Write it down
Note your journey right away. Its meaning often becomes clearer over the following days.

sections.h2: Is shamanic trance safe? Returning and grounding
p: A gentle guided trance is a form of deep relaxation, and you can open your eyes at any moment. Most people find it calming. Still, inner journeys can stir strong images or emotions, so a few habits help.
ul: Always end with a full return: name the room, feel your weight, move your hands and feet.
Drink some water or eat something light afterward if you feel spacey.
Never practice while driving or doing anything that needs your attention.
On days when you feel fragile, choose a simple breathing session instead.
Keep it simple: these journeys need nothing but your attention and a quiet room.

faq: What is a shaman?

A shaman is a person who, in many traditional cultures, enters a trance to communicate with the spirit world on behalf of the community. The word comes from Evenki, a language of Siberia. Shamans may seek guidance, protection or balance for the group, and lead important rituals. Each culture has its own name and practices for this role.
What does a shaman do?

It depends on the culture. Traditionally, a shaman journeys in trance to other worlds to seek guidance or look for the cause of a misfortune. The journey may also aim to recover something lost or to accompany the souls of the dead. Shamans also lead ceremonies and keep the stories of the community. In every case, the journey is made for others, not as a personal adventure.
What is a shamanic journey?

A shamanic journey is an inner voyage made in a trance state, usually to the steady beat of a drum. The traveler enters through an opening, such as a cave or a tree, and explores the lower or upper world. There, they meet allies like power animals, then return by the same path. A guided meditation follows this structure in imagination.
What is shamanic drumming?

Shamanic drumming is a steady, fast, repetitive beat used to support trance. It has no melody, so the mind has nothing to follow but the rhythm. In Siberian traditions, the drum is often called the shaman's horse. A change in rhythm at the end signals the return. Many people find that the beat helps them stay with their inner images.
How do you find your power animal?

In shamanic practice, you find your power animal during a journey, often in the lower world. Set a clear intention, travel inward and notice which animal appears, especially if it shows itself several times. Greet it with respect and ask what it brings you. Afterward, note the encounter, and see whether the same animal returns in later journeys.
What is shamanic healing?

In traditional cultures, what people call shamanic healing is a spiritual role within a whole worldview. Misfortune is often seen as a loss of power, or of part of the soul. The shaman journeys to recover it and restore balance between people and the spirit world. These are cultural beliefs to respect. The meditations in MeditaDream draw on this imagery and make no promise about the body.
Is trance safe?

A gentle guided trance is a form of deep relaxation, and you can open your eyes and stop at any time. To stay comfortable, practice in a quiet place, never while driving, and always finish with a full return to your body. If what comes up weighs on you or keeps returning, ask a professional for advice.
What is core shamanism?

Core shamanism is the approach developed by the anthropologist Michael Harner, author of The Way of the Shaman in 1980. It gathers elements found in many cultures, such as the drum, the journey, the three worlds and the power animal, without the rituals of a specific people. It made shamanic practice accessible in the West, while raising questions of respect.

visualisation.h1: Guided imagery: how visualization works and how to practice
visualisation.lead: Close your eyes and picture a lemon: its color, its weight, the sharp smell as you cut it. That small experiment is mental imagery. Here is how guided imagery works, what research shows and how to visualize better, one sense at a time.
visualisation.def: **Guided imagery** is a practice in which you follow a guide's words to create detailed mental images, using all your senses. You might see a beach, hear the waves, feel warm sand and smell salt in the air. It is used for relaxation, mental rehearsal and meditation, and it can be learned like any other skill.

sections.h2: What is guided imagery?
p: Guided imagery is deliberate mental imagery: you build an inner scene on purpose, led by words. The word imagery can mislead, because it is not only visual. A good guided imagery meditation includes sounds, textures, temperatures, smells and movement.

Mental imagery is something you already do all day. You picture the route to a friend's house, replay a conversation, imagine the taste of a meal. Guided imagery takes that natural ability and gives it a direction.

Psychologists have studied mental imagery for a long time. In 1880, Francis Galton asked people to picture their breakfast table that morning and describe how vivid the image was. Their answers varied enormously, from almost photographic to nearly nothing.

sections.h2: Guided imagery, creative visualization, visualization meditation
p: These terms overlap, and people often use them interchangeably. Each one, though, has its own flavor.
cards: Guided imagery
You follow a guide, in person or in audio, through a scene. The emphasis is on rich sensory detail and relaxation.
Guided visualization
Often used as a synonym. In meditation apps, it usually means a guided scene with a clear intention, such as a walk in a forest.
Creative visualization
Made popular by Shakti Gawain's 1978 book of that name. You imagine a goal as already reached, to clarify what you want and stay motivated.
Visualization meditation
Imagery used as an anchor for meditation. You hold one image steadily, like a candle flame or a mandala, to train attention.

sections.h2: The power of visualization: what research shows
p: Research on motor imagery, imagining a movement without performing it, shows that it engages many of the same brain areas as the real movement. This is one reason mental rehearsal can support learning a skill.

Athlete visualization is the best-known example. Many athletes rehearse a race, a dive or a serve in their minds before they compete. Sport visualization does not replace physical training. Athletes use it alongside, to prepare, to stay focused and to arrive feeling at home in the situation.

Positive imagery, picturing calm or pleasant scenes, is widely used for relaxation, and researchers keep studying when and how it helps. The honest summary: visualization is a real mental skill, rooted in how the brain works. It is not a magic trick.

sections.h2: How do I visualize if I can't see images? Aphantasia
p: Some people see almost nothing when they close their eyes. In 2015, the British researcher Adam Zeman and his colleagues gave this a name: aphantasia, the absence of voluntary visual imagery. At the other end of the spectrum, some people's images are almost as vivid as real sight.

Most people fall somewhere in between, and imagery varies from one sense to another. You might see little but hear clearly, or feel textures vividly. If your visual images are faint, guided imagery still works. Lean on sound, touch and movement, or simply on knowing where you are in the scene.
sections.tip: Do not strain to see. Effort tends to dim inner images, so relax, describe the scene to yourself in words and let the senses that come easily lead the way.

sections.h2: How to visualize better: one sense at a time
p: The most reliable way to train imagery is to work sense by sense, then combine them. This is the progression of the [Visualization](/en/meditations/guided-visualization-meditation.html) category in MeditaDream, six sessions of 16 to 29 minutes.

You start with sight: in Film — a Butterfly Flies Beside You, you follow a butterfly's path and the gust that pushes it off course. Touch comes next, with Touch — the Key in Your Hand: its weight, its coldness, the slight pull when you lift it. Then hearing, with Hearing — the Distant Singing Bowl, where you follow both distance and direction.

Finally, two long sessions bring the three senses together, on the summit of an extinct volcano and in a spaceship's cockpit. The Room You Know asks you to rebuild a familiar room and let the evening light fall into it. When you feel ready, the [Third Eye](/en/meditations/third-eye-meditation.html) category goes further, with images that appear on their own.

sections.h2: Visualization exercises you can try today
p: These visualization techniques take a few minutes each. Do them seated, with your eyes closed, and start with the one that appeals to you most.
steps: The lemon
Picture a lemon in your hand. Feel its weight and its skin, cut it, smell it, bring it to your lips. Notice whether your mouth reacts.
The familiar room
Walk through your bedroom in your mind. Count the objects on a shelf, open a drawer and notice the light.
The object study
Look at a simple object for thirty seconds, close your eyes and rebuild it. Open your eyes, compare and repeat.
The sound map
Imagine a bell ringing far to your left, then closer, then to your right. Follow its position as it moves.
The full scene
Choose a place you love and add one sense at a time: sight, then sound, then touch, then smell.

sections.h2: When to use guided imagery in daily life
p: Guided imagery is not only for long meditations. A few minutes of positive imagery can change the tone of a day. The [4 Minutes](/en/meditations/4-minute-meditation.html) category in the app offers several sessions built on this idea.
ul: Before a challenge: Finding Your Confidence Before a Challenge, 4 minutes, recalls a gesture you already got right.
During a break: Your Instant Refuge, 4 minutes, opens a small place of your own where worries can wait.
On a gray day: A Happy Memory Through Three Senses brings back a good moment through sight, sound and feeling.
When ideas are stuck: Creative Unblocking, 26 minutes, quiets the inner critic and lets ideas come.
In the evening: a world such as The Zen Garden invites you to slow down before the night.

sections.h2: Safe place visualization: your inner sanctuary
p: Safe place visualization is one of the classic guided imagery exercises. You build an inner place where you feel completely at ease: a beach, a forest, a room, a mountain. With practice, simply recalling it can bring back a sense of calm.

Make it precise. What is the ground made of? What sounds are there? Is there a smell, a temperature, an object you like to touch? Some people add a protective symbol, or a presence that keeps them company.

In the app, Your Sanctuary lets you describe this place in detail, from its colors and sounds to an entrance ritual and a return phrase. The worlds also offer ready-made sanctuaries, like [The Floating Island](/en/worlds/floating-island-guided-visualization.html), a small island of your own above the clouds. To explore them all, see the [immersive meditation worlds](/en/worlds/).

sections.h2: Manifestation visualization: an honest look
p: Manifestation visualization is popular online: picture what you want clearly enough, and it will come. Visualization cannot make things appear. Research by psychologist Gabriele Oettingen even suggests that dreaming only of the happy ending can sap the energy to act. Picturing the obstacles as well helps people move forward.

Future Self, in [Consciousness & Trance](/en/meditations/guided-trance-meditation.html), follows this approach: you live the direction you want in imagination, then draw a first concrete step from it. Used this way, visualization helps in three real ways:
ul: It clarifies what you actually want, by turning a vague wish into a concrete picture.
It lets you rehearse the steps, the way an athlete prepares a race.
It keeps your motivation alive on days when the goal feels far away.

faq: What is guided imagery?

Guided imagery is a relaxation and meditation technique in which you follow a guide's words to build a detailed inner scene. It uses all the senses: sight, sound, touch, smell and movement. People use it to relax, to rehearse a skill or an event, and to explore their inner world. It is a learnable skill that grows with regular practice.
How can I visualize better?

Work one sense at a time, starting with the one that comes most easily. Use familiar subjects, like your own room, before imaginary ones. Keep sessions short and relaxed, because straining tends to dim images. Describe the details to yourself in words. With regular practice, most people find their inner scenes become steadier and richer.
How do I visualize if I can't see images?

You are not alone. Some people have little or no visual imagery, a trait called aphantasia, named by Adam Zeman's team in 2015. You can still practice guided imagery through other senses: sounds, textures, temperature, movement, or simply knowing where things are in the scene. Many people with faint images still find guided imagery relaxing.
Does visualization work?

It depends on what you expect. Imagining a movement engages many of the same brain areas as doing it, which is why athletes use mental rehearsal. Calm imagery is widely used for relaxation. But visualization does not make things happen on its own. It works best as preparation, motivation and focus, combined with real action.
How do athletes use visualization?

Athletes use visualization to rehearse a performance in detail before it happens: the start of a race, a jump, a free throw. They imagine the movement, the sensations and the setting, and sometimes possible problems and their response. Sport visualization complements physical training. It helps them prepare, stay focused and feel familiar with the situation when the moment comes.
What is creative visualization?

Creative visualization is the practice of imagining a goal or a desired situation as vividly as possible. Shakti Gawain popularized it with her 1978 book, Creative Visualization. Used well, it helps you clarify what you want and stay motivated. It works best when you also picture the steps and the obstacles, then act on them.
What is a safe place visualization?

A safe place visualization is a guided imagery exercise in which you build an inner place where you feel calm and protected. You fill it with details for every sense. Once it is familiar, you can return to it in a few breaths. In MeditaDream, Your Sanctuary lets you describe this place and keep it on your phone.

sections.h2: What are spirit guides?
p: The idea of a guiding presence is found in almost every culture. It answers a simple human feeling: that help, wisdom or protection can come from somewhere beyond our everyday mind.

The phrase spirit guide became common in nineteenth-century Spiritualism, where mediums spoke of guides who helped them contact the beyond. Today, it is used broadly for any presence that offers spiritual guidance, whatever its form.

The intuition itself is much older. In ancient Athens, Socrates spoke of his daimonion, an inner sign that warned him when he was about to make a mistake. Many traditions since have given this inner wisdom a face and a name.

sections.h2: Guardian angels, ancestors, ascended masters: guides across traditions
p: Each tradition gives guides a different face. Here are the main ones.
cards: Guardian angel

In Christian tradition, each person is believed to be accompanied by an angel. The Gospel of Matthew speaks of children's angels in heaven, and the Catholic Church celebrates guardian angels every October 2.
Ancestors
In many African, Asian and Indigenous traditions, the family's dead continue to watch over the living, and are honored with offerings and remembrance.
Helping spirits
In shamanism, the shaman works with allies met in trance, often in animal form. They protect, teach and guide the journey.
Ascended masters
A notion from Theosophy and its heirs: enlightened teachers said to have lived on Earth and to guide humanity from beyond. The I AM movement spread the phrase in the 1930s.
Higher self
A wiser, deeper part of yourself, described in Theosophy and in many modern spiritual paths. Here, the guide is not outside you but within.
Inner guide
In psychology, a wise inner figure you meet through imagination. Carl Jung described his conversations with such a figure, whom he called Philemon.

sections.h2: Are spirit guides real? Two ways to see them
p: Whether spirit guides exist independently is a question of belief, and no experiment can settle it. What is certain is that many people experience them, and that these experiences can be deeply meaningful.

Psychology offers another reading. Carl Jung developed a method he called active imagination. You let an inner figure appear, then speak with it as if it were real, while staying awake and aware. In this view, a guide is a part of the psyche that knows more than your daily thoughts.

You do not have to choose. In meditation, you can welcome a guide with an open mind. Then judge it by one simple question: does this help me live with more clarity and kindness? The Keeper of the Archives, in [Higher Knowledge & Beyond](/en/meditations/akashic-records-meditation.html), trains this discernment, between what the mind invents and what seems to arise on its own.

sections.h2: Animal spirit guides: how to find your spirit animal
p: Animal spirit guides are among the most widespread. In shamanic traditions, the power animal protects and teaches. Many Indigenous peoples of North America also know totem animals, linked to a person or a clan. The word totem itself comes from Ojibwe.

The phrase spirit animal comes from these Indigenous traditions, and its casual use in pop culture can feel disrespectful to them. Many people now prefer animal guide or power animal. In the app, the guide type is called Spirit Animal.

To find your animal guide in meditation, set the intention, travel to a natural place in imagination and notice which animal approaches. Pay attention to animals that return in your dreams and journeys. [The Wolf Spirit Forest](/en/worlds/wolf-spirit-guided-meditation.html) is built around this kind of encounter, and our page on [shamanic trance](/en/shamanic-trance.html) explains the tradition behind it.

sections.h2: Signs from spirit guides: what people describe
p: People who feel guided often describe the same kinds of signs. Here are the most common, with a gentle reminder to keep both your heart and your mind open. The Journal's Signs & Synchronicities notebook is made to collect them.
ul: Repeated encounters: a bird, an animal or a symbol that keeps appearing.
Synchronicities: meaningful coincidences, like hearing the answer to a question you just asked yourself. Jung coined the word.
A sudden inner knowing, a calm certainty that arrives without reasoning.
Dreams in which a guide speaks, or a figure that returns night after night.
Physical sensations: warmth, a light touch, a feeling of presence.
sections.tip: Write signs down as they happen, then look back after a few weeks. A real pattern holds up over time; a forced one fades.

sections.h2: How to connect with your spirit guides in meditation
p: There are many ways of connecting with spirit guides: prayer, dreams, journaling, walks in nature. Meditation offers a simple, gentle structure. Here is how to meet your spirit guide, step by step. If building the safe place feels hard, our guide to [safe place visualization](/en/guided-imagery-visualization.html) can help. For fully guided versions, the [Spirit Guides](/en/meditations/spirit-guide-meditation.html) category offers five sessions of 16 to 26 minutes.
steps: Go to your safe place
Close your eyes, breathe slowly and imagine a place where you feel completely at ease: a garden, a temple, a shore.
Set an intention
Silently state why you have come: to meet a guide who wishes you well.
Welcome
Notice who or what approaches. It may be a person, an animal, a light or simply a feeling of presence. Greet it with respect.
Ask one simple question
Keep it clear and open, such as: what do I need to know right now? Then listen, without forcing an answer.
Thank
Whatever came, even silence, thank your guide. Gratitude closes the meeting gently.
Return
Walk back the way you came, feel your body and the room, and open your eyes. Write down what you received.
sections.warn: If a figure feels hostile or frightening, you are free to end the meditation, ground yourself and return another day. If such experiences weigh on you or repeat, ask a professional for advice.

p: In the app, a guide can belong to one of eight types: Sage, Spirit Animal, Ancestor, Angel, Shadow, Archetype, Extraterrestrial or Other. The figure below presents six of them.
Do not worry about choosing the right one. A guide's type often becomes clear only after several meetings, and a single guide can surprise you over time.

sections.h2: Keeping a record of your guides
p: Guides tend to reveal themselves over time. One meeting gives you an impression; several meetings give you a relationship. That is why writing things down matters.

In Your Guides, tap New guide to create a page for each guide you meet. How do I know what my spirit animal is?

In shamanic practice, your animal guide shows itself during a journey or a meditation, often several times. You can also notice animals that recur in your dreams, that you feel drawn to, or that cross your path in striking ways. Out of respect for the Indigenous traditions the term comes from, many people say animal guide or power animal.
What are signs from spirit guides?

People commonly describe repeated animals or symbols, meaningful coincidences, a sudden calm inner knowing, recurring dream figures, or a sense of warmth and presence. None of these can be proven, and the mind loves patterns. A good approach is to note signs as they come, then look back after a few weeks to see what really holds.
What is the higher self?

The higher self is a wiser, deeper part of your own being, described in Theosophy and many modern spiritual paths. It is said to see your life with more clarity and love than your everyday mind. Connecting with it usually means quieting down and listening inwardly. In this view, your most trusted guide is not outside you, but within.
What are ascended masters?

In Theosophy and the movements that followed it, ascended masters are enlightened teachers believed to have lived on Earth, then risen beyond it to guide humanity. The phrase was popularized by the I AM movement in the 1930s, in which Saint Germain plays a central role. It is a belief system, with its own texts and followers.
Are spirit guides real?

No scientific method can prove or disprove that spirit guides exist. Believers see them as real beings, while psychology often sees them as inner figures that express a deeper wisdom. Both views agree on one point: the experience can be meaningful. Judge a guide by its fruits. Does it leave you calmer, clearer and kinder?

emotions.h1: Emotional growth: name your feelings, regulate, grow
emotions.lead: Feelings are not problems to solve. They are messages to understand. Here is how emotional growth works in practice. You name what you feel with a feelings wheel, regulate it gently and offer yourself the kindness you would give a friend.
emotions.def: **Emotional growth** is the gradual process of learning to welcome your feelings, name them precisely, understand what they signal and choose how to respond. It is not about feeling less, but about feeling more clearly. It rests on simple skills, such as noticing, naming, self-compassion and emotional regulation, and all of them can be practiced in meditation.

sections.h2: What is emotional growth?
p: Emotional growth is one of the deepest forms of personal growth. It does not mean becoming calm all the time, or never feeling anger or sadness again. It means meeting your feelings with more space and more skill.

You can picture it as four simple movements. In the app, the [Emotional Growth](/en/meditations/self-love-and-gratitude-meditation.html) category follows this path, with eight sessions of 7 to 17 minutes.
cards: Welcome
Let the feeling be there, without pushing it away or drowning in it.
Name
Find the most precise word for it: not just “bad,” but disappointed, lonely or ashamed.
Understand
Ask what it is telling you: a need, a value, a limit that was crossed.
Choose
Decide what to do, or not do, now that you see more clearly.

sections.h2: Plutchik's wheel of emotions
p: In 1980, the psychologist Robert Plutchik proposed a model of eight basic emotions: joy, trust, fear, surprise, sadness, disgust, anger and anticipation. He arranged them in a wheel, each one facing its opposite. Joy faces sadness, trust faces disgust, fear faces anger, and surprise faces anticipation.

Each emotion comes in degrees. Annoyance can grow into anger, then rage. Serenity can deepen into joy, then ecstasy. Neighboring emotions also combine: joy and trust give love, while anticipation and joy give optimism.

sections.h2: How to use a feelings wheel
p: A feelings wheel, or emotion wheel, helps you move from a vague state to a precise word. Plutchik's is one model. Another, widely shared, is the Feeling Wheel created by Gloria Willcox in 1982. Its center holds six core feelings: sad, mad, scared, joyful, powerful and peaceful. The outer rings offer finer nuances.
steps: Start at the center
Ask yourself which broad family your feeling belongs to: anger, fear, sadness, joy…
Move outward
Look at the finer words in that family and pick the one that fits best, such as frustrated, jealous or hurt.
Check in your body
Notice where you feel it: a tight jaw, a heavy chest, a warm face. The body often confirms the right word.
Name it kindly
Say it inwardly: “I'm feeling hurt.” Simply naming the feeling is already a step.

sections.h2: Naming your feelings: the first step of emotional growth
p: The psychologist Matthew Lieberman and his team at UCLA studied what happens when people put feelings into words. In brain scans, labeling an emotion reduced activity in the amygdala, a region involved in emotional reactions. They called this affect labeling.

In plain words: name it to tame it, as the saying goes. The more precise the word, the more room you have around the feeling. This is why a feelings wheel is so useful, and why journaling can feel calming. In [Learning Basics](/en/meditations/meditation-for-beginners.html), the session Distinguishing Sensation, Emotion, and Thought — the Three Layers of Experience trains exactly this.

Naming is also the root of emotional intelligence, an idea popularized by Daniel Goleman's 1995 book of that name. Goleman describes a set of skills: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills. All of them begin with noticing what you feel.

sections.h2: Emotional regulation techniques for daily life
p: Emotional regulation is the ability to influence how strongly you feel and express your emotions, and how long they last. It is not suppression. Research suggests that simply pushing a feeling down rarely makes it go away. Regulation is more like learning to ride the wave.

Here are a few ways to regulate emotions that you can use anywhere. For hot moments, the [4 Minutes](/en/meditations/4-minute-meditation.html) category offers sessions of 3 to 4 minutes, such as Calming Down After an Argument.
ul: Slow your breathing, with an out-breath longer than the in-breath.
Name the feeling, as precisely as you can.
Ground yourself: feel your feet, look around and name five things you see.
Step back: look at the scene as if from a little distance, or from a week from now.
Move your body: walk, stretch or splash cool water on your face.
Wait before acting. A pause of a few breaths changes many decisions.

sections.h2: How to process emotions in a healthy way: a meditation
p: Processing an emotion means letting it move through you until it settles, instead of avoiding it or replaying it endlessly. In everyday language, this is often what people mean by emotional healing: moving through hard feelings rather than around them. Here is a simple meditation for it.
steps: Pause
Sit down, close your eyes or lower your gaze, and take three slow breaths.
Find it in the body
Where is the feeling? Throat, chest, belly? Notice its size, its temperature and its movement.
Name it
Give it the most precise word you can find, without judging it.
Make room
Breathe around the sensation, as if giving it more space. You do not need to change it.
Listen
Ask what it needs. The answer may be rest, a boundary, a conversation or simply time.
Be kind
Place a hand on your heart and offer yourself a few kind words, as you would to a friend.
Return
Open your eyes, notice the room and see whether the feeling has shifted, even slightly.
sections.warn: If a feeling is too strong to sit with, or keeps coming back, you do not have to face it alone. Ask a professional for advice.

sections.h2: Self-compassion and self-love: learning to love yourself
p: Kristin Neff, a researcher at the University of Texas at Austin, describes self-compassion in three components. Self-kindness means speaking to yourself with warmth rather than harsh judgment. Common humanity means remembering that struggle and imperfection are part of every human life. Mindfulness means seeing your difficult feelings clearly, without exaggerating or ignoring them.
With Christopher Germer, Neff developed the Mindful Self-Compassion program, now taught in many countries. Its core idea is simple: offer yourself the care you would give a good friend.

Self-love grows from there. It is not vanity, and it does not mean believing you are perfect. Learning to love yourself means recognizing your real qualities, like perseverance or curiosity, and caring for yourself as someone worth caring for. Developing Self-love, a 15-minute session, starts exactly there.

sections.h2: Gratitude, forgiveness and shadow work
p: Gratitude trains your attention to notice what is going well, which a stressed mind tends to overlook. A few precise lines each evening are enough. Our page on the [gratitude journal](/en/gratitude-journal.html) shows how to keep one.

Forgiveness is often misunderstood. It does not mean excusing or forgetting. It means deciding what you want to carry, and what you are ready to set down. The session Forgiving Without Forgetting lets you decide for yourself, while keeping what you learned.

Shadow work, an idea inspired by Carl Jung, means meeting the parts of yourself you usually avoid, such as anger, envy or shame. Seen with kindness, they often turn out to be protecting something. The [Shadow & Well-being](/en/meditations/shadow-work-meditation.html) category offers ten sessions for this, from Shadow Work to Inner Child Serenity.
